newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban bring Islamic hope and force to Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Taleban bring Islamic hope and force to Kabul.

text.p: Black-bearded Taleban militia warriors swarmed into Kabul on Friday at the climax of a two- year campaign to drive out "corrupt" Mujahideen guerrilla factions and then enforce a strict Islamic rule on Afghanistan.
Wild-eyed and battle-grimed, the Islamic rebels took over this city of one million people with little bloodshed, after troops loyal to President Burhanuddin Rabbani fled northwards.
The people of Kabul, who have endured more than four years of factional fighting and destruction, awoke to find the Taleban in full control.
"I am happy they are here," said Nazia, a women in her 50s wrapped in a dirty white chaddar. "I have been to bed several times on an empty stomach, I had no food or money."
She was walking towards the gate of the presidential palace, where crowds jostled throughout the day to gaze at the hanged bodies of a former president, Najibullah, and his brother.
Taleban gunmen abducted Najibullah from the U.N. compound where he had been since the Mujahideen toppled his communist government in April, 1992.
"He deserved his fate," Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, the top Taleban leader in Kabul, told reporters.
"The message is clear. Anyone who works against Islam will meet the same fate."
Inside the sprawling presidential compound, weary Taleban fighters rested, prayed and milled around, posing for cameras and careering about in jeeps and pick-up trucks.
The Taleban, who burst on the Afghan scene in 1994 from Islamic colleges in Pakistan, now control most of the country.
The former government's military chief, Ahmed Shah Masood, has retreated to his stronghold of Jabal-us-Seraj, 70 km (45 miles) north of Kabul.
It was not clear if he could hold it now that the Taleban have captured military airbase at Bagram.
The Taleban say they would impose the same Islamic strictures, including amputation of hands for theft, as they have elsewhere in Afghanistan.
"Now there will be an Islamic army and an Islamic life and you will see the change," Rabbani said.
People in Kabul, where many women are educated and work in government offices, the change will be a shock.
Rabbani said only male government employees should report to work. A decision on when and how women could work would be made later. Girls could only go to school "within an Islamic framework".
For the moment, Kabul is heaving a brief sigh of relief as the battered city has been spared another bloodbath.
The value of equally battered currency lept immediately.
Money changers near Pul-i-Khishti mosque were offering only 11,000 afghanis to the dollar, compared to 18,500 afghanis 24 hours earlier.
"We think that the afghani will go up further when the market opens tommorrow," said Rasheed, an elderly currency dealer.

The streets were crowded with pedestrians and cyclists within hours of the Taleban takeover as the tension that had built up during the Taleban's lightening advance from Sarobi, 60 km (40 miles) east of Kabul, ebbed away.
Taleban commanders rejected their enemies' accusations that aid from neghbouring Pakistan explained the victory.
"When we have God on our side, why should we need Pakistan?" asked commander Musa at a military barracks on the northern edge of the city.
